title: Unsecured Credentials: Chat Messages
summary: Chat and collaboration platforms are a routine channel for sharing working credentials. Engineers paste database passwords, API keys and access tokens into direct messages, team channels, incident threads and ticket comments, where the material persists in the platform's history and search index. Rather than hunting files on disk, an adversary with access to a user endpoint, an administrator portal or an integration token can query the service directly for keywords such as password, key or token, and can abuse workflow and bot integrations to sweep channel history automatically. Slack and Teams token theft, or a session cookie lifted from a browser profile, gives the same result without touching the client. Detection centres on platform audit logs, especially unusual search patterns, mass message export, new integration tokens and logins from unexpected locations.

beginner.definition: This technique is about finding passwords and keys that people wrote in chat messages. A coworker may send a login to a colleague, or paste an access key into a support ticket. An attacker who can read those conversations, or search them, collects the secrets.
beginner.whyItMatters: People share secrets in chat because it is quick and feels private. Those messages stay on the server for years and are easy to search. One stolen chat account can reveal keys for many systems. This is why chat is now a common place attackers look first.
howItWorks: People paste passwords, keys or tokens into chat messages and ticket comments.
The chat service stores every message on its servers and indexes the words.
An attacker steals a user session, a bot token or an administrator login.
The attacker searches the stored history for words such as password or token.
Automated workflow tools can search every channel and quietly copy matches out.
The attacker uses the collected secrets to reach other systems and services.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk where staff write handover notes on a whiteboard. Someone writes the code to the drug cabinet there so the next shift can find it fast. Visitors in the waiting room can read the board from the corridor. Nothing was hacked; the secret was simply left where many people could see it. Chat channels are that whiteboard, and the audience is larger than anyone expects.
takeaways: Never send passwords or keys through chat; use an approved secrets manager.
Watch chat audit logs for unusual searches, exports and new integration tokens.
Rotate any credential that was ever shared in a message or ticket.

objectives: Explain how credentials end up stored in chat and collaboration platforms.
Describe the difference between reading chat logs on disk and querying the service directly.
Identify audit log events that reveal suspicious message searches or exports.
Recognise the risk created by bot and workflow integrations with broad message access.
Recommend practices that keep secrets out of chat conversations.
